clue.text: Something devised by many in the French camp

parts.note: le is the French for 'the'

indicators.note: the word in tells us the 'many' letter goes inside the word for camp

parts.note: camp in the sense of flamboyantly effeminate, an old sense of gay
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred, hence many

explanation.surface: A scheme cooked up by a crowd within a French military camp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Devised' is the legal sense: to devise property is to leave it by will, so the thing devised is what a will bequeaths.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, to devise is to bequeath real property by will, so a bequest is something devised.

clue.text: "So, qu'est a manger, Louis?" or, perhaps, "Is this le chef's bible?"

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the quoted words and the 'or' could be rearranged into something else

parts.note: the quoted franglais question is taken letter by letter as fodder
the little word or between the two quotations is fodder too

explanation.surface: Two mock-French remarks about a hungry Louis and a cook's essential reference book.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram fodder is all nineteen letters of the first quotation plus the two of 'or', which looks like a mere connective between the two quotations.
explanation.definitionFit: This famous French culinary encyclopaedia is the standard reference for professional cooks, a chef's bible.

clue.text: At day's end could be all in, say, but rising with a will

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means the piece is read upwards, from bottom to top

parts.note: say is a common pointer to 'for example', abbreviated eg

indicators.note: could be signals that the words all in may be rearranged
the end of the word day's is its final letter

explanation.surface: Someone exhausted at the close of the day nonetheless gets up eagerly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns EG into GE; 'could be' rearranges ALL IN into NIALL; 'end' of day's gives Y, placed last although the clue mentions it first.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something with a will means doing it heartily and good-humouredly, close to cheerfully or warmly.

clue.text: C-cacophonous cautionary condition

parts.note: the stammered opening letter of the clue supplies the letter C as written
cacophonous means harshly noisy, that is loud

explanation.surface: A stammered warning about a noisy situation to beware of.
explanation.walkthrough: The stutter 'C-' is not decoration: it gives the first letter, followed by a synonym of cacophonous.
explanation.definitionFit: Being under a cloud is a state of suspicion or disgrace, a condition that warns others to be wary.

clue.text: Champ on motorbike with gas in it. O, calamity!

indicators.note: calamity suggests a disaster that throws the preceding letters into disorder

parts.note: these words are taken letter for letter as anagram fodder
the exclamation O is a letter of the fodder

explanation.surface: A motorcycle champion's machine catches fire with fuel inside, a disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: Giacomo Agostini was the Italian rider who won fifteen motorcycle world championships.
explanation.definitionFit: Agostini is one of the most successful motorcycle racing world champions ever.

clue.text: See 1 down
Cutter cut between Liverpool and Manchester?

parts.note: a cutter is a small sailing vessel, so a ship
a cut is an old word for a man-made waterway

explanation.surface: A question about a boat cutting through the land between two north-west English cities.
explanation.walkthrough: The Manchester Ship Canal links Manchester to the Mersey estuary near Liverpool; 'cut' is a traditional British name for a canal.
explanation.definitionFit: The famous waterway built so seagoing vessels could reach inland Manchester from Liverpool's estuary.

clue.text: His 'air, say, removed with hot wax treatment

definitions.text: His 'air, say, removed with hot wax treatment

parts.words: His 'air, say, removed with hot wax treatment
parts.note: read as a beauty-salon waxing, but 'air said as heir points to the son of Daedalus, killed when the sun melted the wax of his wings

explanation.surface: A dropped-aitch remark about someone's hair being waxed off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'His 'air, say' sounds like 'his heir': Daedalus's son, who flew too near the sun so the wax holding his wings melted.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth this boy, Daedalus's heir, died when hot sun melted the wax of his feathered wings.

clue.text: King Mark's bride upped and left in Day One

indicators.note: in tells us the left letter is put inside the turned phrase
in a down clue, upped means the pieces are read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: Tues is the usual abbreviation for Tuesday, a day
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A royal bride got up and walked out on her first day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upped' turns TUES + I into ISEUT, and 'in' puts L inside. In the Tristan legend she is the Irish princess who marries King Mark of Cornwall.
explanation.definitionFit: In Arthurian legend this Irish princess was wed to King Mark of Cornwall while loving Tristan.

clue.text: Take over! Play the music!

parts.note: R is the abbreviation of recipe, Latin for 'take', used on prescriptions
over can mean on, as in a lid placed over or on a jar
to do a play or a part is to perform it

explanation.surface: Two brisk commands to a band: take charge and strike up.
explanation.walkthrough: R for 'take' comes from the Latin recipe heading old prescriptions.
explanation.definitionFit: A rondo is a musical form whose main theme keeps returning between contrasting episodes.

clue.text: Spicated, you say, otherwise barbed

indicators.note: otherwise suggests the letters arranged in a different way

parts.note: the word is taken letter for letter as anagram fodder
the letter U is pronounced like the word you

explanation.surface: A spiky term, as one might put it, or else something with hooks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'you say' gives U because the letter sounds like the word; it joins SPICATED as fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuspidate describes something ending in a sharp point, like a barb or fang.

clue.text: Never a cross word during this match?

definitions.text: Never a cross word during this match?

parts.words: Never a cross word during this match?
parts.note: a crossword-free union read slyly: a wedding with no quarrels, and one at a register office where no cross, the Christian sign, is involved

explanation.surface: A wry question about a marriage in which nobody ever argues.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'cross word' is both an angry word and the Christian cross absent from a secular ceremony; 'civil' also means polite.
explanation.definitionFit: A wedding performed by a registrar without religious rites, and literally a polite partnership.

clue.text: Such a door on Dick Fosbury's garage?

definitions.text: Such a door on Dick Fosbury's garage?

parts.words: Such a door on Dick Fosbury's garage?
parts.note: a garage door type that swings upward is matched with the high jumper who went backwards over the bar

explanation.surface: Wondering what kind of garage door a famous high jumper would own.
explanation.walkthrough: Dick Fosbury was the American high jumper whose 'Fosbury flop' took him up and over the bar backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A common style of garage door that tilts upward and back over the opening, apt for a high jumper.

clue.text: C-cast clod

parts.note: the stammered opening letter of the clue supplies the letter C as written
to cast is to throw, or hurl

explanation.surface: A stammering instruction to throw a lump of earth.
explanation.walkthrough: As in the companion clue, the stutter supplies the opening letter. 'Clod' is the boor, not the lump of soil.
explanation.definitionFit: A churl is a rude, boorish person, as is a clod.

clue.text: Redeeming feature of 22 3

parts.note: the two cross-referenced entries combine into the opening of a proverb about bad times having a good side

explanation.surface: Bare cross-references asking for the good side of something.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the two cross-referenced answers together and complete the well-known proverb that begins with them.
explanation.definitionFit: The proverb says every gloomy situation has a hopeful or comforting aspect, a redeeming feature.

clue.text: Poet certified Prisoner of Zenda, up or out

indicators.note: out suggests the letters are thrown out of their order

parts.note: the word is taken letter for letter as fodder
these words are fodder too

explanation.surface: A poet declared insane and the famous adventure novel about a prisoner.
explanation.walkthrough: The American poet was declared insane and confined after his wartime broadcasts; 'Prisoner of Zenda' is a novel title.
explanation.definitionFit: This American modernist poet was held for treason and certified insane, confined in a hospital for years.

clue.text: Hat once quietly tipped here?

indicators.note: tipped means tipped out, the letters spilled into a new order

parts.note: these words are taken letter for letter as fodder
p, piano, is the musical direction for quietly

explanation.surface: Asking whether this is where hats were once silently raised in respect.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue defines too: men tipped their hats in silence at the memorial in Whitehall.
explanation.definitionFit: A war memorial, where people traditionally doffed hats in quiet respect for the dead.

clue.text: "A dreadful thane!" (some of Macbeth's curse)

indicators.note: dreadful suggests the word thane is knocked out of shape

parts.note: the word is taken letter for letter as fodder

indicators.note: some of tells us to take just the opening part of the next word

explanation.surface: An exclamation about a terrible Scottish lord, with a note that it is part of his curse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dreadful' rearranges THANE into NATHE; 'some of' takes only the first letters of Macbeth's.
explanation.definitionFit: An anathema is a formal ecclesiastical curse or denunciation.

clue.text: Town where Elgar meant very little, right? Wrong!

indicators.note: Wrong! signals that the letters before it are in the incorrect order

parts.note: these words are taken letter for letter as fodder
v is the abbreviation for very, a very little version of the word

explanation.surface: A claim about the town where Elgar mattered little, swiftly corrected.
explanation.walkthrough: The town is in Worcestershire, where the composer Edward Elgar lived and is buried nearby, so the surface claim is false.
explanation.definitionFit: A spa town in Worcestershire, in the Malvern Hills, closely linked with Elgar.

clue.text: He sculpted "The Speaking Compass". When?

indicators.note: speaking tells us we hear the words rather than see them spelt

parts.note: compass in the sense of range, or scope; as can mean when, as in 'as I left'

explanation.surface: A sculptor credited with a talking navigation instrument, and a date is asked.
explanation.walkthrough: Scopas was a Greek sculptor of the fourth century BC who worked on the Mausoleum at Halicarnassus.
explanation.definitionFit: Scopas was an ancient Greek sculptor and architect, famed for expressive marble figures.

clue.text: A Ford Granada blowout

definitions.meaning: a small family car made by the Ford Motor Company
a party or festival in a Spanish city, a blowout being a lavish celebration

explanation.walkthrough: The Granada was also a Ford model, which makes the surface about one car.
explanation.definitionFit: It is both a long-running Ford hatchback and the Spanish word for a festive celebration.

clue.text: Primate uniting church with devil

parts.note: an imp is a little devil

explanation.surface: A primate who brings together a church and a demon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Primate' could be an archbishop, which the church in the surface encourages; here it is an ape.
explanation.definitionFit: A chimpanzee is an ape, one of the primates.

clue.text: Cheese in France: what for? All round nonsense!

indicators.note: all round tells us the nonsense word surrounds the other pieces

parts.note: rot is a word for nonsense
que is the French word for what
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone asks what a French cheese is for, and dismisses it all as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in France' marks the French word for 'what'; 'All round' wraps the nonsense word about it and the English 'for'.
explanation.definitionFit: A famous blue sheep's milk cheese from southern France.

clue.text: One and all so English? On the contrary

indicators.note: on the contrary tells us the two pieces come in the opposite order to the clue's

parts.note: so as in 'so good', meaning very

explanation.surface: Asking whether everyone is so English, then denying it.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue offers 'so English', VERY then E; 'On the contrary' flips the order.
explanation.definitionFit: Every means each single one without exception, that is one and all.

clue.text: Lay down rough pale stout

indicators.note: rough suggests the words are roughed up into a new order

parts.note: these words are taken letter for letter as fodder

explanation.surface: Lie down after a rough pale stout.
explanation.definitionFit: To postulate is to assume or lay down something as a basis for argument.

clue.text: Cheer up "… with our English dead!"

parts.note: the late means the dead

explanation.surface: A rallying cry quoting Henry V's speech about closing the breach with the English dead.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation is from Shakespeare's Henry V: 'Or close the wall up with our English dead'.
explanation.definitionFit: To elate is to fill with joy, to lift someone's spirits.

clue.text: It separates arches from cusp and relic

indicators.note: from tells us the letters are taken out of the following words

explanation.surface: Something from a church vault distinguished from its cusps and relics.
explanation.walkthrough: The triangular space between neighbouring arches is a familiar term in church architecture.
explanation.definitionFit: A spandrel is the roughly triangular space between the curves of two adjacent arches.

clue.text: More epigrammatical, say, than this oracular medium

indicators.note: say tells us to hear the word rather than read it

parts.note: more epigrammatical means terser and more pointed, that is pithier

explanation.surface: Comparing someone's terse wit with that of an oracle.
explanation.walkthrough: The Pythia was the priestess of Apollo at Delphi.
explanation.definitionFit: She was the priestess at Delphi who spoke the god's oracles, a medium for prophecy.
